data.title: Detva – Kalamárka, a guard hillfort above the Detva basin
data.excerpt: On a columnar andesite spur above Detva, in the foothills of the Poľana massif, stands Kalamárka — the only Early Medieval site known in the Detva basin. Rock faces up to 25 m high protect almost its whole perimeter; a rampart 50 m long closed the one open approach. The hillfort guarded the mountain passage into the Zvolen basin from the 9th century until the Kingdom of Hungary took the region over.

children.text: The excavation of the upland site of Kalamárka, some 5 km north of Detva in the Detva foothills of the Poľana massif, was carried out by Peter Šalkovský. It is the only Early Medieval site known so far in the Detva basin (east of Zvolen), and one that has repeatedly been the centre of attention of amateur “researchers”, which has steadily diminished its evidential value.

Šalkovský reports that the site is formed by a columnar andesite spur (803–816 m above sea level) with a summit plateau (about 0.9 ha) protected on three sides (about 88 % of the perimeter of the site) by vertical rock faces 8–25 m high. Only on the east, where the ground slopes down into a flat mountain saddle, was it necessary to build a rampart some 50 m long above a natural break in the terrain.

Kalamárka, sometimes also known as Chrapková or Hrabková, is one of the longest-known archaeological sites in central Slovakia; interest in it goes back to the 19th century. Modern excavation has confirmed repeated settlement of the site from the Late Bronze Age through the Hallstatt, La Tène and Roman periods and the Migration Period down to the Early Middle Ages. As much as 91 % of the finds come from the interior enclosure, most of them from the zone behind the rampart (56 %) and the central part of the acropolis (27 %), where the only settlement feature was also uncovered — a sunken-featured building on a dry-stone footing (5.7 × 3.2 m). The fewest finds (8 %) come from the south-western spur of Kalamárka. Only 9 % of the finds come from the flat saddle below the hillfort, and no finds at all from the trial trenches west of it, which shows that there was minimal interest in using the areas outside the protected enclosure for settlement.

children.text: Strategically well placed, Kalamárka attracted people as early as prehistory. It was settled by a succession of cultures, for the first time in the Late Bronze Age by the Lusatian and Kyjatice cultures. As the excavation showed, the oldest fortification dates only from the very end of the Bronze Age. The site was also settled by the Celts, and it was later used by the Germanic Quadi at the time when the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius was fighting against them in our territory. It attracted the attention of the Slavs as early as the period when the Avar Khaganate was collapsing and the Principality of Nitra was emerging, which — besides pottery — is attested by finds of a tongue-shaped belt end-fitting and a belt loop belonging to the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon, with several parallels from the first third to the first half of the 9th century in south-western Slovakia and in Moravia. Although the excavation found no trace of a fortification from that period, the finds of the Blatnica–Mikulčice type indicate the presence of a socially privileged class. The main phase of settlement and the attested fortification work belong to the Late Great Moravian to post-Great Moravian period.

The Early Medieval rampart was built on substantial remains of a prehistoric, or rather protohistoric, fortification whose surface had apparently been partly worked over and levelled. The total width of the rampart in its upper part was 440–450 cm. The core of the rampart was filled with earth, mostly strongly burnt at a secondary stage, and reinforced by a timber structure that cannot be specified more closely — perhaps a transverse grillage — indicated by sporadic oak charcoal and the remains of a beam. The total length of the rampart was about 50 metres, and in its southern part, very poorly preserved, a break for an entrance may be assumed. Ramparts of this so-called shell construction are the main type of Great Moravian fortification, applied at many hillforts of the late 8th to 10th centuries throughout the middle Danube region and in Bohemia. An atypical element in the Detva structure is the use of an inner stone wall, which occurs only occasionally and in rudimentary form (Majcichov, Spišské Tomášovce, Strachotín) and was usually replaced by a timber wall. This type of rampart, originally termed Přemyslid, was widespread with various deviations across the whole West Slavic territory. Pottery finds in the fill and in the underlying layer of the rampart date its construction to the Late Great Moravian to post-Great Moravian period (end of the 9th to the 10th century).

children.text: A total of 2,040 potsherds were analysed. The most archaic pottery types have their models at settlements and hillforts of the 8th to the first half of the 9th century (Prša, Sliáč, Vyškovce nad Ipľom, Hradec). These are simply profiled smaller pots with rounded or simply obliquely cut rims, rather imperfectly wheel-finished and clumsily decorated. Most of the pottery is the technologically more advanced production known from settlements of the second half of the 9th to the 10th century (Ipeľský Sokolec, Slovenské Ďarmoty, Zvolen, Bojnice, Tlmače, Hronský Beňadik): more strongly profiled, with better executed decoration, above all combed. The latest and technologically most progressive material is at the same time the least numerous. It consists mainly of larger pots with obliquely to vertically cut, cornice-like everted rim edges, or with a thickened grooved rim, decorated with more grooves and spiral lines. This material cannot be placed earlier than the 10th/11th century (Hronský Beňadik, Bíňa). Among the other artefacts (72 pieces) there are weapons — the most interesting of them an iron double-edged sword — together with pieces of equipment, arrowheads, buckles, a strap-end and a horseshoe, as well as agricultural and craft tools and household equipment (such as a sickle, a quern, small chisels, fire-steels, whetstones, spindle whorls, small knives and an axe), and building and hanging fittings such as nails, cramps and a key, which can broadly be placed in the 9th to 11th centuries.

children.text: On the basis of the excavations, Šalkovský states that the site can on the whole be interpreted as a small upland hillfort guarding, from a forward and strategically advantageous position, the mountain passage from the Ipeľ region along the Kriváň valley into the Zvolen basin. It was inhabited from the beginning of the 9th century, and certainly during the period of the threat from the early Hungarians, in the period of the so-called White Croatian principality and perhaps also later, at the time of Bohemian and Polish interventions and of the political domination of Slovakia (10th to the first half of the 11th century). The vigorous defensive, military and political activity of the late Great Moravian power structures and their heirs in the region of central Slovakia, rich in mineral resources, is further illustrated — besides the Detva hillfort — by other fortifications, such as the hillfort at Zvolen-Môťová 20 km to the west (10th–11th century) at the mouth of the road from Krupina to Zvolen, as well as the group of three hillforts at Tlmače, Malé Kozmálovce and Hronský Beňadik (end of the 9th to the 10th century), which closed the Hron route into central Slovakia.

In conclusion, Šalkovský notes that the scanty written sources relating to the 10th and 11th centuries suggest that the regions of central and northern Slovakia were occupied by the Árpáds and joined to the Kingdom of Hungary only after the so-called Polish–Hungarian settlement (1018) and the death of Bolesław the Brave in the second half of the 11th century. Once the situation of state formation in the Carpathian Basin had stabilised, the hillfort at Detva lost its strategic importance and was no longer settled. The exceptional standing and historical importance of the Detva guard hillfort is underlined by its forward position on the eastern edge of the Detva basin, which until the late Middle Ages was only a sparsely settled part of the Zvolen comitatus. The core of the settlement area it served lies 20 to 30 km further west, in the Hron region, which was better placed for settlement and farming.

The significance of the Kalamárka hillfort is presented today by a nature trail. It can be reached by bicycle or by car to the car park below the forester’s lodge along the concrete-panel road from the hamlet of Stavanisko, or on foot along the red waymarked trail from Stavanisko. By car you can get to within about 200 m of the hillfort. There are several well-made information panels at the hillfort from which the visitor learns what they need to know about the history of this exceptional place.
